paragraphs: Friend, here's what I take from Tyre. God starts by quoting the city's own words: "I am perfect in beauty." (Ezekiel 27:3) Then He lays out the cedar, the oak, the ivory, the linen, the warriors and the trading partners from every coast, and every piece of it is impressive. The lesson is that you can have a gorgeous ship and a full cargo hold and still be sailing on what you say about yourself.

Look at where the wind comes from. "Your oarsmen have brought you onto the high seas, but the east wind will shatter you in the heart of the sea." (Ezekiel 27:26) Tyre's own crew rowed it out there, and all that heavy cargo couldn't hold it up. I think that's the warning for you and me: wealth, skill and good looks are fine things to have, but they make a lousy place to hide. I spent years as a worn-out stamper with blurry edges, and trust me, the things that make us look impressive are not what hold us up.

Now listen to how the story ends. The sailors don't cheer. They "weep over you with anguish of soul and bitter mourning," and the kings of the earth shudder with fear. (Ezekiel 27:31, 35) Even the people who got rich off Tyre can see how big the fall is. So the next time you catch yourself admiring your own shiny ship, baker, ask what you're really counting on to carry it, because God's word through Ezekiel says the sea doesn't care how good the cargo looks.
